title: Plate Tectonics: Volcanoes, Earthquakes & Tsunamis
description: How the Earth's moving plates create volcanoes, earthquakes and tsunamis — and why people choose to live in hazardous places.

notes.heading: 📌 Inside the Earth
notes.body: The Earth is made of four main layers. The crust is the thin, solid outer shell we live on. Oceanic crust (under the oceans) is only about 5-10 km thick but dense; continental crust (under the continents) is thicker (30-70 km) but less dense. Below the crust lies the mantle, a layer of very hot rock about 2,900 km thick. The upper mantle behaves like a very slow-moving liquid — it can flow over millions of years. At the centre is the core, made mainly of iron and nickel. The outer core is liquid and the inner core is solid, with temperatures around 5,500 degrees C — as hot as the surface of the Sun. Radioactive decay in the core releases heat, which drives slow convection currents in the mantle. These currents are the engine that moves the plates above them.

notes.heading: 🔑 Continental Drift and Plate Tectonics
notes.body: In 1912, Alfred Wegener proposed the theory of continental drift: the continents were once joined in a single supercontinent called Pangaea and have slowly drifted apart. His evidence included the jigsaw-like fit of coastlines (South America and Africa), identical fossils of the same species found on continents now separated by oceans, matching rock types and mountain ranges on different continents, and glacial deposits in places that are now hot. Other scientists rejected his idea because he could not explain HOW the continents moved. We now know the answer: the crust is broken into about 15 large slabs called tectonic plates, which float on the semi-molten mantle and are moved by convection currents at a few centimetres per year — about the speed your fingernails grow. Most volcanoes, earthquakes and fold mountains are found along the edges (boundaries) of these plates.

notes.heading: 🔑 Types of Plate Boundary
notes.body: There are three main types of plate boundary. At constructive (divergent) boundaries, plates move apart. Magma rises to fill the gap, cools and forms new crust, creating mid-ocean ridges and gently sloping volcanoes. Example: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge — Iceland sits on it and is being slowly pulled apart. At destructive (convergent) boundaries, plates move together. Where oceanic crust meets continental crust, the denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the lighter continental plate — a process called subduction. The sinking plate melts, and the magma can rise to form explosive volcanoes. Subduction also creates deep-sea trenches and can fold rocks into mountains (the Andes). Where two continental plates collide, neither can sink, so the rock crumples upwards into fold mountains like the Himalayas. At conservative (transform) boundaries, two plates slide past each other. No crust is created or destroyed, so there are no volcanoes — but the plates often jam and then jerk free, causing powerful earthquakes (the San Andreas Fault in California).

notes.heading: 📎 Volcano Types and Eruptions
notes.body: Volcano shape depends on the type of lava. Shield volcanoes erupt runny (basaltic) lava that flows long distances before cooling, building wide, gently sloping cones. Eruptions are frequent but usually mild. Example: Mauna Loa in Hawaii, found near constructive boundaries and hotspots. Composite volcanoes (stratovolcanoes) erupt thick, sticky (andesitic) lava that sets quickly, building steep-sided cones. Gas cannot escape easily from sticky lava, so pressure builds up and eruptions are explosive. Example: Mount St Helens (USA), found at destructive boundaries. Eruptions can produce lava flows, clouds of ash, pyroclastic flows (super-fast avalanches of hot gas and rock, up to 700 degrees C), lahars (mudflows when ash mixes with water) and volcanic gases. Volcanoes also bring benefits: ash weathers into fertile soils, geothermal heat can generate electricity, and eruptions attract tourists and produce valuable minerals.

notes.heading: 🔑 Earthquakes: Focus, Epicentre and Measurement
notes.body: An earthquake is a sudden release of energy when plates that are locked together finally slip. The point underground where the earthquake starts is the focus (hypocentre); the point on the surface directly above it is the epicentre, where shaking is usually strongest. Energy travels outwards as seismic waves, recorded by instruments called seismometers. Two scales are used to describe earthquakes. The Richter scale measures magnitude — the energy released — from the size of the seismic waves. It is logarithmic: each whole number up means about 10 times more ground movement (and roughly 30 times more energy). The Mercalli scale measures intensity — the observed effects on people and buildings — from I (not felt) to XII (total destruction). The Mercalli scale varies from place to place for the same earthquake, while magnitude is a single number. Earthquakes cannot yet be predicted, but scientists can identify the areas most at risk.

notes.heading: ⚠️ Tsunamis: Formation and Warning
notes.body: A tsunami is a series of giant ocean waves, usually triggered when an undersea earthquake at a destructive boundary suddenly pushes a section of the sea floor up or down, displacing the whole column of water above it. (Underwater landslides and volcanic eruptions can also cause them.) In the deep ocean, a tsunami travels at up to 800 km/h — as fast as a jet plane — but the wave may be less than a metre high, so ships barely notice it. As the wave reaches shallow coastal water it slows down and the water piles up into waves that can be tens of metres high. A common warning sign is the sea suddenly drawing back from the beach, exposing the sea floor, minutes before the wave strikes. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami (caused by a magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Indonesia) killed around 230,000 people in 14 countries, and the 2011 Tohoku tsunami in Japan caused the Fukushima nuclear disaster. Today, warning systems use seismometers to detect earthquakes and ocean buoys (such as the DART system) to confirm a wave, then alert coastal populations to evacuate to high ground.

notes.heading: 💡 Effects, Responses and Living with Risk
notes.body: The effects of tectonic hazards are divided into primary effects (caused directly by the event, such as buildings collapsing, deaths from shaking or lava, and roads being destroyed) and secondary effects (the knock-on consequences, such as fires from broken gas pipes, disease from contaminated water, and long-term homelessness and economic loss). Responses are split into short-term responses (search and rescue, emergency shelter, food and medical aid — hours to weeks) and long-term responses (rebuilding to safer standards, improving prediction, monitoring and preparation, such as seismic sensors, volcano observatories, building codes, hazard maps, evacuation drills and sea walls). Preparation is usually cheaper and more effective in richer countries, which is why a similar-magnitude earthquake often kills far more people in a poor country. Yet millions of people still live near hazards. Reasons include fertile volcanic soils, geothermal energy, mineral wealth, tourism jobs, cheaper land, family and cultural ties, poverty that limits choices, and the belief that it will not happen to me.

flashcards.definition: The thin, solid outer layer of the Earth that we live on. Oceanic crust is thin and dense; continental crust is thicker but less dense.
flashcards.example: Oceanic crust is about 5-10 km thick, while continental crust can be 30-70 km thick.

flashcards.definition: The layer of very hot, semi-molten rock between the crust and the core, about 2,900 km thick, which flows very slowly.
flashcards.example: Convection currents in the mantle drag the tectonic plates along above them.

flashcards.definition: A slow circular movement in the mantle: hot rock rises, cools, and sinks again, transferring heat from the core and moving the plates.
flashcards.example: Heat from radioactive decay in the core drives convection currents that push plates apart at mid-ocean ridges.

flashcards.definition: A plate boundary where two plates move apart and magma rises to create new crust, forming mid-ocean ridges and gentle volcanoes.
flashcards.example: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs through Iceland, which is being pulled apart at a few centimetres per year.

flashcards.definition: The process at a destructive boundary where a denser oceanic plate sinks beneath a less dense plate and melts in the mantle.
flashcards.example: The Pacific Plate subducts beneath Japan, producing deep earthquakes and explosive volcanoes.

flashcards.definition: A plate boundary where two plates slide sideways past each other. No crust is made or destroyed, but friction causes earthquakes.
flashcards.example: The San Andreas Fault in California, where the Pacific and North American plates grind past each other.

flashcards.definition: A wide, gently sloping volcano built from runny basaltic lava that flows far before cooling; eruptions are frequent but mild.
flashcards.example: Mauna Loa in Hawaii is one of the largest shield volcanoes on Earth.

flashcards.definition: A steep-sided volcano built from layers of sticky lava and ash; trapped gas makes its eruptions explosive and dangerous.
flashcards.example: Mount St Helens (USA, 1980) erupted explosively, blowing off the side of the mountain.

flashcards.definition: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus (the underground starting point) of an earthquake, where shaking is usually strongest.
flashcards.example: Rescue teams are sent first to settlements closest to the epicentre.

flashcards.definition: A logarithmic scale measuring the magnitude (energy released) of an earthquake; each whole number means about 10 times more ground movement.
flashcards.example: A magnitude 7 earthquake shakes the ground about 10 times more than a magnitude 6.

flashcards.definition: A series of huge ocean waves usually caused by an undersea earthquake displacing a column of water; waves grow taller as they reach shallow water.
flashcards.example: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed around 230,000 people across 14 countries.

flashcards.definition: The immediate impacts of a hazard caused directly by the event itself, as opposed to secondary effects which happen as knock-on consequences.
flashcards.example: Buildings collapsing during shaking is a primary effect; a fire started by broken gas pipes is a secondary effect.

questions.stem: Which list shows the layers of the Earth in order from the surface to the centre?
choices: Crust, core, mantle
Crust, mantle, outer core, inner core
Mantle, crust, core
Core, mantle, crust
questions.explanation: Starting at the surface: the crust is the thin outer shell, the mantle lies beneath it, and the core (liquid outer core, solid inner core) is at the centre.

questions.stem: Which of these was used by Alfred Wegener as evidence for continental drift?
choices: The same fossils are found on continents now separated by oceans
Volcanoes erupt along plate boundaries
Satellites can measure plate movement
The inner core is made of solid iron
questions.explanation: Identical fossils and matching rocks on widely separated continents suggested they were once joined. Satellite measurement of plate movement came long after Wegener's time.

questions.stem: What feature forms where two plates move apart under the ocean?
choices: A deep-sea trench
Fold mountains
A mid-ocean ridge of new crust
A subduction zone
questions.explanation: At a constructive boundary, plates separate and magma rises to fill the gap, solidifying into new crust and building a mid-ocean ridge such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

questions.stem: At a destructive boundary, why does the oceanic plate sink beneath the continental plate?
choices: Because it is thinner and denser
Because it is hotter
Because it is made of continental crust
Because convection currents push it upwards
questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is denser than continental crust, so when the two collide the heavier oceanic plate is forced down into the mantle — the process called subduction.

questions.stem: Which type of plate boundary has earthquakes but NO volcanoes?
choices: Constructive
Destructive
Conservative
Collision
questions.explanation: At a conservative boundary plates slide sideways past each other, so no crust is created or melted — meaning no magma and no volcanoes, only earthquakes from the friction.

questions.stem: Why do composite volcanoes have steep sides?
choices: Their runny lava flows a long way before setting
Their thick, sticky lava sets quickly and does not travel far
They are made entirely of ash from one eruption
They erode faster at the base than at the top
questions.explanation: Sticky (andesitic) lava cools and solidifies close to the vent, building up layers of lava and ash into a steep cone. Runny lava creates the gentle slopes of shield volcanoes instead.

questions.stem: Why are composite volcanoes usually more explosive than shield volcanoes?
choices: They are taller, so gravity is stronger
Gas escapes easily from their lava, building no pressure
Gas cannot escape easily from thick, sticky lava, so pressure builds until it explodes
They only erupt under the sea, where water flashes to steam
questions.explanation: Sticky lava traps dissolved gases. Pressure builds beneath the blockage until it is released violently. Runny shield-volcano lava lets gas escape steadily, so eruptions are gentler.

questions.stem: What is the epicentre of an earthquake?
choices: The point underground where the earthquake starts
The point on the surface directly above where the earthquake starts
The instrument that records seismic waves
The line where two plates meet
questions.explanation: The earthquake starts at the focus underground; the epicentre is the surface point directly above it, where shaking and damage are usually greatest.

questions.stem: On the Richter scale, a magnitude 6 earthquake produces roughly how much more ground movement than a magnitude 5 earthquake?
choices: Twice as much
About 10 times as much
About 100 times as much
Exactly the same — the scale is not about movement
questions.explanation: The Richter scale is logarithmic: each whole-number increase means about 10 times more ground movement (and roughly 30 times more energy released).

questions.stem: Two cities experience the same earthquake. City A reports Mercalli intensity VIII and City B reports Mercalli intensity IV. What does this tell you?
choices: The cities experienced different earthquakes
The Mercalli scale measures observed damage, which varies with distance and building quality, while the magnitude is the same everywhere
City A must be nearer the focus underground
The Richter scale is inaccurate for this earthquake
questions.explanation: Mercalli intensity records the effects actually observed at each location, which depend on distance from the epicentre, ground type and building standards. One earthquake has a single magnitude but many intensities.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of a tsunami?
choices: A storm at sea whipping up large waves
An undersea earthquake suddenly displacing a column of water
Melting ice caps adding water to the ocean
A ship striking an underwater volcano
questions.explanation: Most tsunamis are triggered when an earthquake at a destructive boundary jerks the sea floor up or down, displacing all the water above it. Storm waves are much smaller and only affect the surface layer.

questions.stem: A tsunami in the deep ocean is travelling at 800 km/h but is less than a metre high. What happens to it as it approaches a coastline?
choices: It speeds up and flattens out
It slows down and grows much taller as the water piles up in the shallows
It disappears because waves need deep water
It turns back out to sea
questions.explanation: In shallow water the base of the wave drags on the sea floor, slowing the wave front. The water behind catches up and piles upwards, building waves that can be tens of metres high.

questions.stem: Which of these is a SECONDARY effect of an earthquake?
choices: A building collapsing during the shaking
A road cracking open when the ground moves
A fire spreading afterwards because gas pipes broke in the shaking
A person killed instantly by falling masonry
questions.explanation: Secondary effects are knock-on consequences that follow the event, such as fires from broken gas pipes or disease from contaminated water. Collapse during shaking is a direct, primary effect.

questions.stem: Millions of people live on the slopes of active volcanoes. Which is the STRONGEST set of genuine reasons why?
choices: Volcanoes are safe because eruptions can always be predicted exactly
Fertile soils, geothermal energy, tourism jobs and family ties — combined with poverty limiting the choice to move
Volcanic ash makes the air healthier to breathe
Governments pay people to live in hazard zones
questions.explanation: Volcanic areas offer real benefits — rich soils for farming, geothermal power, minerals and tourism — while poverty, land costs and family or cultural ties can leave people with little practical choice. Eruptions cannot be predicted exactly.

questions.stem: A coastal country prone to earthquakes wants to reduce deaths from future disasters. Which of these is a LONG-TERM response rather than a short-term one?
choices: Sending search-and-rescue teams after an earthquake strikes
Distributing emergency food and tents to survivors
Rebuilding schools to earthquake-resistant standards and running regular evacuation drills
Setting up field hospitals for the injured
questions.explanation: Long-term responses happen over months and years and focus on preparation: safer building codes, monitoring, hazard maps and drills. Rescue, emergency shelter and field hospitals are immediate, short-term responses.
